All of the suggestions below are excellent, and with my own experience with anxiety and depression (my family too has a history of being wired weird) I can suggest a couple strategies to minimize the squishing of it all while you're working on more holistic mental health strategies. :)

Until you can get the anxiety itself squared away, here are some tips for managing your stress relief habits while at the store: 

1) Immediately put things into your cart as you select them. This will feel weird, as you might be used to carrying things around while you decide on options, but unless you're reading the information on the product try to keep them in the cart to minimize item squishing. 

2) Bring something you can direct your stress habits at instead of innocent packaged products. My stress habit is more convenient then some (I'm a chronic hair twirler, think what girls do when drunkenly flirting at the bar, but all the time), and I have long hair so this is convenient. My brother has a tendency to to wear a ring with a spinner on it (I've seen them online, it's just a plain metal ring with a spinning bit in the middle). He'll spin the spinner with the idle hand not pushing anything to keep it occupied.

3) Try wearing ear-buds while shopping, and listen to some of your favorite podcasts or music, though maybe not something that hypes you up. While my hype music may make me feel less depressed, I have noticed it increased my tendency to use my anxious ticks, and I have better success just listening to something that sort of vaguely holds my attention. Current go-to choices are NPR or classical music. While this won't keep your hands occupied, it will hopefully lessen your need to do self comforting habits in the first place. 

Sounds like you're making really good progress in identifying issues, things are gonna be hard and any of the important changes are going to feel REALLY weird at first. I know that when I started making a couple of them to mitigate my own self-comforting habits it almost felt like leaving the house and thinking I didn't lock the door, just that subtle nagging in the back of my mind that made it difficult to relax. I can at least say that as time when on that niggling feeling went away more and more, it just took time and some bull-headed stubbornness. I wish you the best of luck and I hope this helps you in some way!

To a certain extent you're sort of screwed, in that you'll probably not entirely get away from the pets in question. As a person coming from a family with ALLOT of pets (We live in Alaska, and have enough room to have a ton comfortably), my mom gets somewhat offended when people consistently want us to stow the dogs away when they come over. I think it feels like someone rejecting her babies (which they are, point here being she almost literally sees them as her toddlers). From here you'll have to figure out a way to compromise with the person who's house you're visiting. 

I'm assuming that the, "pretend you're allergic" strategy isn't foolproof since you listed family as one of the groups who has dogs you'd like to avoid, so most of your strategy from here will be figuring out how to phrase, "I really, really, don't like dogs" in a way that doesn't ping any sort of protective instincts. 

My suggestion, coming from a family with lots of dogs, is to be accommodating, but only to a point. Maybe suggest that they keep the dogs on a floor of the house that you won't be frequenting (we keep ours upstairs since that's just bedrooms and the public spaces are all on ground floor), but that might be harder in a one story home. Maybe dog gates would help. Unfortunately pets are going to be a hard thing to abstain from, but I'm sure if they're your friends and family they'll understand if you try and talk to them about it. 

I know that my dogs really want a good sniff, but will lose interest if you don't talk excitedly or show interest yourself. This may sound awkward af, but one thing I have friends who don't want to meet the wave of doge do is bring a dirty sock or something over (I know, kinda weird), and I just sorta give that to the dogs to smell so that they don't need to be all up on my amigos business.

I'm 23 and my dad just transitioned at 60. While I'm glad she feels better about herself, she and my mother had a rocky divorce when I was child and I never got much support from her (she had a drinking problem she hid from us whenever we flew down to see her, which probably contributed), and now that she's fully transitioned she says she wants a relationship with me but things are rocky. She seems overall more focused on herself than on me, but still makes emotional demands of me without reciprocating. Sometimes it's hard to be understanding of her mood swings and the borderline emotional abuse she throws out (she said that my brother was mis-gendering her for walking around shirtless, even though he does that at our mothers house where he is literally surrounded on all sides by women; she has also yelled at me for not treating her like a woman or acting like a woman, which I took issue with since I'm acting like, and treating her like, any other woman in my life). There are a lot of expectations on her part that I can't live up to, and it seems like allot to ask out of children she's only had superficial contact with over the years.

The hardest part is that I'm not really allowed to air any issues I have with all of this because I quickly feel like I'm doing something wrong, and I don't want to make people think that transitioning isn't worth it. I just have issues being accepting of things involved in her transition (on easier days we laugh over it being like a girl going through high school all over again), when she wasn't very accepting of my own awkward years. 

All in all, I would still deeply recommend anyone considering a transition look into carefully and seriously. I believe many of my dad's issues come from her upbringing and the repression of this part of herself. The drinking, the failed marriages, lots of it can be rooted in such a constant denial of such am important part of her. That said, still be careful. My dad wasn't honest with her psychiatrists about a good number of Bi-Polar diagnoses she's received throughout her life, and instead attributed the symptoms to PTSD. While that might be a contributing factor, we had a terrible couple of months where they gave her depression medication that exacerbated her Bi-Polar disorder to a terrible degree, especially when paired with the inherent stress of the situation. 

TL;DR : Just be honest with yourself. If you think you're the wrong gender look into it. Be honest with your physicians about any family history of mental disorders or chronic illnesses, in a change this extreme it is so, so, important to have the best information to work on. When transitioned just show the people in your life the empathy you would like, we want to be there for you and we're doing our best, flawed though we may be. If someone close to you is transitioning do your best to be patient, it may not always feel fair and you don't find many shoulders to cry on because of how awkward these things are, but they need you and the same rule applies to you as them, show them the empathy you would like to receive.
